title: Stage 7 — Data Modeling
goal: Grow your schema with relationships, indexes, pagination, and search — without restarting the project.
summary: One-to-many, many-to-many, indexes, and query params — same repo, richer data model.

checkpoint.prompt: Each workout belongs to one category. In the workouts table, `category_id` should…

choices.text: Reference the categories table (foreign key)
Store the category name as plain text only
Be optional on every row with no link

checkpoint.explanation: Foreign keys enforce relationships at the database level and enable efficient joins.

checkpoint.prompt: A workout can have many tags, and a tag can belong to many workouts. How do you model that?

choices.text: A junction table (workout_tags) linking workout_id and tag_id
Store all tag names in one TEXT column on workouts
Duplicate the workouts table for each tag

checkpoint.explanation: M:N needs a join table with two foreign keys — one row per workout–tag pair.

checkpoint.prompt: You filter `WHERE name LIKE '%run%'` on 50,000 rows and it's slow. What helps?

choices.text: An index on the filtered/sorted columns (when appropriate)
Delete half the rows
Change HTTP to GET-only

checkpoint.explanation: Indexes speed up lookups and sorts. They're not magic — but they matter as tables grow.

checkpoint.prompt: GET /workouts?page=2&limit=20 — what does the API return differently from page 1?

choices.text: The next slice of results (rows 21–40), not the full table
A completely different database
Only HTTP headers, no body

checkpoint.explanation: Pagination limits payload size and query cost. Page + limit select a window of rows.

checkpoint.prompt: GET /workouts?q=run — what should the API do with `q`?

choices.text: Filter rows with a parameterized WHERE (e.g. name LIKE)
Concatenate q directly into SQL without escaping
Ignore q and return all rows always

checkpoint.explanation: Search is a filtered query — always use placeholders, never string-concat user input.

checklist.label: Related table with foreign key (e.g. categories → workouts)
Junction table for M:N (e.g. workouts ↔ tags)
List endpoint supports ?page= and ?limit= with metadata
List endpoint supports ?q= with parameterized SQL filter
At least one index on a column you filter or sort by

questions.prompt: You need categories on workouts. Best approach?

choices.text: ALTER / CREATE in the same repo — migrate forward, don't wipe the DB
Delete the repo and start a new tutorial
Store categories only in frontend localStorage

questions.explanation: Real projects evolve schema in place. Stage 8 adds formal migration files.

questions.prompt: One category, many workouts — where does the foreign key go?

choices.text: On the many side (workouts.category_id → categories.id)
On the one side (categories.workout_id)
Foreign keys are not used in SQL

questions.explanation: The "many" side holds the FK pointing to the "one" side.

choices.text: A junction table with workout_id and tag_id
A JSON array column only — no extra table
Merging both tables into one

questions.explanation: Each row in the junction table is one link between one workout and one tag.

choices.text: Faster responses and less memory when tables grow large
SQL cannot return more than one row
Browsers forbid arrays over 10 items

questions.explanation: Pagination keeps payloads bounded. Clients load more as the user navigates pages.

choices.text: Use a ? placeholder in LIKE — never concat user input into SQL
Build SQL with template literals from req.query.q
Run q as raw SQL from the client

questions.explanation: Search filters are still SQL — parameterized queries prevent injection.
